=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel: Buyer Review of Seller's SPA Positions and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

## Overall assessment

The Seller's package moves most of the risk on the known diligence issues onto Wattlebridge. Three positions work together to do this:

1. **General disclosure** of the whole data room and the public registers.
2. **A broad buyer-knowledge exclusion** (clause 8.3) that covers constructive knowledge and adviser knowledge.
3. **Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance** that apply to "all Claims of any nature".

Together, these mean we would probably have no warranty claim for any of the issues the Disclosure Letter itself identifies. Those issues are Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay, the bonuses, the data incident and the Sandbar renewals. The fix is not just to soften the warranty limitations. Each known issue needs its own remedy: a price adjustment, a condition precedent or completion deliverable, or a specific indemnity outside the general regime.

The Seller's cover letter also contradicts its own Disclosure Letter on several points. For example, it says Bluefen is "addressed" while the Disclosure Letter says no consent has been delivered. It calls the incident "not material" while the Disclosure Letter says the scope is unknown. These contradictions are useful negotiating leverage.

## Preliminary point: the "FINAL / not to be re-opened" framing

The preamble says these positions were "settled at principal level by both deal teams" and are "not intended to be re-opened". That is the Seller's assertion, not something I can treat as established. It also conflicts with the same letter's invitation to provide our "mark-up".

- **Action:** Confirm internally whether Wattlebridge principals agreed any of these points, and on what terms, before we treat anything as closed. Unless a signed term sheet or heads of agreement says otherwise, I am treating every point below as open.
- The "market context" figures (10–20% cap, ~1% basket, 12–18 months) are Seller advocacy. Some fall within ranges that are often seen. However, "market" is a starting point for negotiation, not a reason to accept a term. It also says nothing about how the terms should apply to known, specific risks, which is where the real exposure sits.

## Material issues

### 1. Buyer knowledge exclusion (cl 8.3): highest priority

**Seller position:** No claim for any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, "including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records."

**Problems:**
- It covers *constructive* knowledge ("discoverable"). That is wider than disclosure itself and requires no fair disclosure standard at all.
- It covers *advisers'* knowledge, which captures everything in our lawyers', accountants' and technical advisers' files.
- Combined with general disclosure, it largely empties the warranties of value.
- It would bar claims on exactly the issues we have identified.

**Push back:**
- Replace it with an express statement that the Buyer's rights are not affected by any knowledge, actual, constructive or imputed, other than matters Fairly Disclosed in the Disclosure Letter.
- **Fallback:** Limit it to the *actual* knowledge of named individuals on the Wattlebridge deal team, at signing, that the specific facts *constitute a breach*. Specific indemnities must apply regardless of knowledge.

### 2. General disclosure (Disclosure Letter [1.1]–[1.2], Schedule 7)

**Seller position:** Everything in the data room as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, plus the Accounts, statutory registers and public corporate records, is disclosed against every warranty.

**Problems:**
- It disclosures against the warranties wholesale. The Accounts warranties, for example, become qualified by the Accounts themselves.
- The data room cut-off is now about six weeks old. We need to know what has been added since, and what has changed.
- "Publicly searchable corporate records" is open-ended.

**Push back:**
- Allow only specific disclosures in the Disclosure Letter that meet a "Fairly Disclosed" standard. That means sufficient detail for a reasonable buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter and assess its impact.
- At most, allow data room documents to be deemed disclosed only where the Disclosure Letter specifically references them.
- No general disclosure against fundamental, tax or title warranties.
- No new disclosure against warranties repeated at Completion. Alternatively, any supplementary disclosure should give us a termination right or a claim, and must not cure a breach.
- Paragraph [1.4] (non-admission) is acceptable in principle. It must not be read as limiting the specific indemnities.

### 3. Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance applying to "all Claims of any nature" (cl 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5)

**Problem:** As drafted, these could reach fraud, specific indemnities, completion covenants (including debt repayment), leakage and restrictive covenants. Exclusion of liability for fraud is unlikely to be enforceable in any event. Non-reliance clauses also may not fully protect a seller against misleading or deceptive conduct claims under the Australian Consumer Law (s 18). Even so, the drafting should be explicit.

**Push back:** Carve out:
- fraud, dishonesty, wilful misconduct and deliberate concealment by the Seller or its representatives;
- specific indemnities;
- the tax indemnity;
- title and capacity warranties;
- covenants and Completion obligations, including the price and debt mechanics.

### 4. Cap (cl 12.1): 20% (AUD 4.8m)

The cap may be negotiable for general warranties in isolation. It becomes unacceptable when combined with the Seller's other positions, because the same cap would then also apply to title, tax and the known issues.

**Push back:**
- **General warranties:** Seek more than 20%, for example 30–35%. Treat 20% as a concession we might give in exchange for the carve-outs below.
- **Fundamental (title and capacity) and tax:** 100% of the Purchase Price.
- **Specific indemnities:** Either 100% of price or uncapped, depending on the item. They must not erode the general cap.
- **Fraud:** Uncapped.

### 5. Thresholds (cl 12.2): de minimis AUD 25,000; basket AUD 250,000, recoverable only above the basket

**Problem:** A 250k basket is about 1.04% of price, at the top end of the Seller's own claimed range. It is also a *deductible* basket: we absorb the first AUD 250,000 even after the threshold is crossed. A 25k de minimis without aggregation lets a series of related small claims escape.

**Push back:**
- Make it a **tipping basket**, so that once the threshold is reached, recovery runs from the first dollar.
- Lower the basket to about 0.5% (AUD 120,000).
- Lower the de minimis to about AUD 10,000, with related claims aggregated.
- Thresholds should not apply to fundamental, tax, specific indemnity or fraud claims.

### 6. Time limits (cl 12.3 / 13): 18 months, applied "to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise"

**Problem:** The default wording quietly pulls title, tax and indemnity claims into the 18-month period.

**Push back:**
- **General warranties:** Accept 18–24 months. A period spanning at least one full audit cycle after Completion is the key point.
- **Tax:** At least the relevant statutory amendment period plus a buffer. Typically 5–7 years.
- **Title and capacity:** 7 years.
- **Specific indemnities:** Periods tied to each risk. For example, privacy matters should run until regulatory and third-party exposure has fallen away.
- **Default rule reversed:** General limitations apply to general Warranty Claims *only*.

### 7. Fundamental / title and capacity warranties under the general cap and time limits

"Administrative simplicity" is not a reason to cap title at 20% of price. If title fails, we have paid AUD 24m for less than we bargained for.

**Reject.** Title and capacity warranties should be capped at 100% of price, run for 7 years, and sit outside the de minimis, basket and disclosure.

### 8. Title evidence (DD-012)

The share register alone is not enough. The Disclosure Letter ([10]) itself says we have not verified it.

**Require:**
- an ASIC company extract reconciled to the register;
- the constitution, and any shareholders' agreement or rights of first refusal or pre-emption;
- confirmation that there are no options, convertible notes, SAFEs or ESOP grants (relevant to the DD-005 bonus arrangements);
- PPSR searches against both the Seller and the Company.

**Key point:** Check whether the Riverlark security includes a share mortgage or other security over the shares given by Harbourglass. If it does, a release must be delivered at Completion, not afterwards (see issue 10).

### 9. Bluefen change-control consent (cl 3 / 6.3)

**Facts:** About AUD 3.6m of FY26 revenue (~30%) comes from Bluefen. Its contract has a change-control consent clause (cl 11.2) with conditions (cl 11.3). The Disclosure Letter confirms that *no* final consent has been obtained and there is *no* evidence the conditions are satisfied. The cover letter's claim that this is "addressed" is wrong on the Seller's own disclosure.

**Problems with the Seller's mechanism:**
- "Reasonable endeavours" is too weak.
- Treating the condition as "satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent" ignores the cl 11.3 conditions. It would also accept a consent that is qualified or comes with conditions, such as repricing or new termination rights.

**Push back:**
- Make it a **condition precedent for the Buyer's benefit, waivable only by the Buyer**. The condition should require unconditional written consent from Bluefen, or consent on terms acceptable to the Buyer acting reasonably, and evidence that the cl 11.3 conditions are satisfied.
- The Seller should use all reasonable endeavours. The Buyer should approve the consent request before it goes, and have the right to attend discussions with Bluefen.
- Include a long-stop date and a Buyer termination right.
- Add a warranty that Bluefen has not given notice of termination, non-renewal or material reduction in volumes.
- Given the concentration, consider a price adjustment or earn-out / deferred component linked to Bluefen retention if consent comes with adverse terms.

### 10. Riverlark facility (cl 2 / 7): about AUD 3.2m, release "following Completion"

**Problem:** This conflicts with the debt-free/cash-free basis. The facility has a change-control clause (cl 8.1), so Completion may itself trigger a default or acceleration. If the release only arrives after Completion, the Company would be in default under a secured facility we now own, and the security would still be registered.

**Push back:**
- Treat the Riverlark amount as Debt, including accrued interest, break costs and fees, deducted from the price. It should be paid directly to Riverlark from the Completion funds flow.
- **Completion deliverables:**
  - a payoff letter, specifying the payout figure and per diem;
  - a deed of release and discharge of all security, including any share security;
  - an undertaking to lodge PPSR financing change statements, or lodgement at Completion;
  - return of title documents;
  - the cl 9.2 discharge.
- Alternatively, obtain a Riverlark waiver of cl 8.1 before Completion. Repayment at Completion remains the cleaner outcome.

### 11. DD-005 Completion bonuses: AUD 420,000, omitted from the funds flow

**Problem:** The Seller calls these "a matter for the Seller". However, the Company is the employer, so it bears the payment obligation and the on-costs. Those on-costs are not quantified and include:
- PAYG withholding;
- superannuation guarantee, if the bonuses are ordinary time earnings (likely, as bonuses tied to employment generally are);
- NSW payroll tax;
- possibly workers compensation.

If a continued-employment condition means a bonus is payable *after* Completion, the cost falls on the Company under our ownership.

**Push back:**
- Treat the bonuses plus all employer on-costs as **Transaction Costs / Debt-like items** deducted from the price. This applies whether they are payable at or after Completion.
- Payments at Completion should go through Company payroll. Amounts payable later should be held in escrow or retained.
- Obtain a specific indemnity covering any related tax or superannuation shortfall.
- Ask for the bonus agreements themselves. Confirm there are no other change-of-control or retention payments, and no equity-style rights.

### 12. Ironquay IP (cl 11.1): indemnity "limited to the specific SOW3 payment"

**Problem:** Under DD-004 cl 7.3, Project Materials transfer only on cleared payment of *every* SOW3 fee. DD-010 shows AUD 180,000 open, and there is no payment receipt or confirmatory assignment. Until all fees are paid, Ironquay may own SOW3 materials that could be embedded in the core product.

Indemnifying only the payment amount ignores the real exposures:
- infringement claims;
- injunctions;
- re-development costs;
- customer claims if the product is disrupted.

The 180k may also not be the only outstanding SOW3 fee, since the condition covers "every" fee.

**Push back:**
- **Condition precedent or Completion deliverable:**
  - evidence of cleared payment of all SOW3 fees, at the Seller's cost or deducted from the price;
  - written confirmation from Ironquay that nothing further is owed;
  - an executed confirmatory IP assignment, with moral rights consents where relevant.
- A specific indemnity for **all Loss** relating to Ironquay and SOW3 IP ownership. It should sit outside the cap, basket, time limits, disclosure and knowledge exclusion, or have its own high cap and a long period.
- Clarify through technical diligence which SOW3 materials are in production code.

### 13. DD-006 export / privacy incident (cl 4.6 / Schedule 6)

**Facts:** A download link was sent to an unintended external email address. The export may contain about 1,240 records: names, business emails, roles and activity timestamps. It is unknown whether anyone accessed the file, and the scope and any notification obligation have not been determined. The Seller calls this "not expected to be material". The Disclosure Letter says the investigation is only preliminary.

**Concerns:**
- **Notifiable Data Breaches scheme:** Under the *Privacy Act 1988* (Cth), an entity that suspects an eligible data breach must complete a reasonable and expeditious assessment, generally within 30 days. The disclosure is dated 22 September and it is now 5 November. We need to know when the incident was discovered and whether the assessment window has passed. Paperbark's status as an APP entity and the date it became aware are threshold questions.
- **Customer contracts:** The data may belong to customers, possibly including Bluefen. Customer contracts may impose their own notification duties and liabilities.
- **Penalties:** The penalty and enforcement framework has been strengthened recently. Regulatory exposure should not be assumed to be minor.

**Push back:**
- **Information request:**
  - the full incident timeline;
  - forensic and access logs;
  - the recipient's identity, any response, and any deletion confirmation;
  - the NDB assessment and notification decision;
  - customer communications;
  - whether insurers have been notified.
- A specific indemnity for all Loss from the incident, including regulatory penalties to the extent legally indemnifiable, investigation, notification and remediation costs, and third-party and customer claims. It should sit outside the general limitations and the knowledge exclusion.
- A pre-Completion covenant requiring the Seller to complete the assessment and make any required notifications, in consultation with the Buyer.
- Add privacy and cyber warranties, with this incident specifically disclosed but not general carve-outs.

### 14. Sandbar supplier renewals: three × AUD 110,000 (AUD 330,000 aggregate)

**Problem:** The Disclosure Letter says to read DD-008 and DD-011 "together for timing/scope". That points to one commitment possibly split into three, each below a threshold. The threshold could be one in the conduct-of-business covenant, a material contracts definition, or internal approval limits. "Related" also needs clarifying: related to each other, or a related-party arrangement? The Seller does not say whether the renewals are terminable, unavoidable, accrued or prepaid. Calling them "ordinary course" is an assertion, not a fact.

**Push back:**
- Ask for the documents, renewal dates, termination rights and any relationship between Sandbar and the Seller or its affiliates.
- If the renewals were entered or renewed after the accounts date or locked period, or outside the ordinary course, require one of:
  - Buyer consent;
  - termination before Completion at the Seller's cost; or
  - treatment of unaccrued committed amounts as Debt-like.
- Tighten the conduct-of-business covenant so related commitments are aggregated when applying thresholds.
- If any related-party element exists, treat it as leakage or Debt and add a related-party warranty.

### 15. Office lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009)

The Seller's description that these involve "notification only" and "no consent on share sale" should be checked against the underlying documents, not accepted as stated.

**Action:**
- Many leases and commercial contracts treat a change in control as an assignment. Review both definitions of assignment.
- Make any lease notification a pre-Completion covenant or Completion deliverable.
- If either document does contain a change-of-control trigger, add it to the consents conditions.

### 16. Tax and IP "under the general regime"

**Reject.**
- **Tax:** Require a standalone tax indemnity or covenant for pre-Completion tax, including tax arising from the bonuses and any payroll tax or superannuation shortfall. It should be capped at 100% of price, with a 5–7 year period, conduct-of-claims provisions, and no general disclosure.
- **IP:** For a SaaS target, the IP warranties should be fundamental or near-fundamental, with an elevated cap and a longer period. This is especially important given Ironquay. They should cover ownership of the code, open-source compliance, and employee and contractor assignments.

### 17. Credit support

Harbourglass is a ventures vehicle that may distribute sale proceeds soon after Completion.

**Seek:**
- an **escrow or retention**, for example 10% of price for 18–24 months, plus specific holdbacks for Ironquay and DD-006; and/or
- a parent guarantee.

Note that W&I insurance, if we pursue it, will typically exclude known and disclosed matters. That means everything above must still be covered by the Seller directly.

## Indicative exposure from known items

| Item | Amount | Proposed treatment |
|---|---|---|
| Riverlark debt | ~AUD 3.2m plus interest and break costs | Debt; paid out at Completion |
| DD-005 bonuses | AUD 420k plus on-costs | Debt-like / Transaction Costs |
| Ironquay SOW3 | AUD 180k (minimum) plus IP risk | Paid pre-Completion plus specific indemnity |
| Sandbar renewals | Up to AUD 330k | Investigate; Debt-like or terminate if not ordinary course |
| DD-006 incident | Unquantified | Specific indemnity plus escrow |
| Bluefen | ~AUD 3.6m revenue p.a. at risk | Condition precedent; possible price or earn-out protection |

About **AUD 4.1m of identifiable amounts** sit outside the Seller's proposed funds flow or warranty regime, before the Bluefen and privacy risks are counted. That is roughly 17% of price, close to the Seller's entire proposed cap.

## Summary of recommendations

1. **Do not accept the "FINAL" framing.** Confirm internally what, if anything, principals agreed.
2. **Delete the buyer-knowledge exclusion (cl 8.3),** or limit it to the actual knowledge of named individuals. It should never apply to indemnities.
3. **Replace general disclosure with specific, Fairly Disclosed matters.** No updating disclosure at Completion that cures a breach.
4. **Carve out from all limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance:** fraud, fundamental warranties, tax, specific indemnities and covenants.
5. **Split the liability regime by claim type:**
   - General warranties: a cap above 20%, a tipping basket of about 0.5%, a de minimis of about AUD 10k with aggregation, and 18–24 months.
   - Title, capacity and tax: 100% of price, 7 years for title, 5–7 years for tax.
   - Specific indemnities: their own terms.
6. **Bluefen:** A Buyer-waivable condition precedent requiring unconditional consent and satisfaction of the cl 11.3 conditions, with all reasonable endeavours, a long-stop date and a termination right.
7. **Riverlark:** Repay from the price at Completion, with a payoff letter, deed of release and PPSR discharge as Completion deliverables. No post-Completion release.
8. **Bonuses:** Deduct the AUD 420k plus all on-costs as Debt-like items, with a tax indemnity.
9. **Ironquay:** Payment of all SOW3 fees and a confirmatory IP assignment before Completion, plus a full-Loss specific indemnity.
10. **DD-006:** A full information request, a pre-Completion covenant to complete the NDB assessment, a specific indemnity, and an escrow holdback.
11. **Sandbar:** Investigate whether the renewals were split and whether there is a related-party element. Treat them as Debt-like or require termination if not ordinary course, and aggregate commitments in the conduct-of-business covenant.
12. **Title:** Independent verification through ASIC, PPSR (including any share security) and the constitution.
13. **Lease and Mossvale:** Verify the change-of-control definitions ourselves, and make the lease notification a Completion deliverable.
14. **Credit support:** A general escrow or retention plus specific holdbacks, and/or a parent guarantee.
15. **Refresh diligence:** Obtain all data room additions since 22 September 2026.

*These views are based only on the Seller documents provided. The underlying DD documents and the full SPA draft should be reviewed to confirm them. NSW-qualified counsel should sign off the final positions, particularly on enforceability, the Privacy Act notification timing, and payroll tax and superannuation treatment.*

- No general disclosure against fundamental, tax or title warranties.
- No new disclosure against warranties repeated at Completion. Alternatively, any supplementary disclosure should give us a termination right or a claim, and must not cure a breach.
- Paragraph [1.4] (non-admission) is acceptable in principle. It must not be read as limiting the specific indemnities.

### 3. Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance applying to "all Claims of any nature" (cl 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5)

**Problem:** As drafted, these could reach fraud, specific indemnities, completion covenants (including debt repayment), leakage and restrictive covenants. Exclusion of liability for fraud is unlikely to be enforceable in any event. Non-reliance clauses also may not fully protect a seller against misleading or deceptive conduct claims under the Australian Consumer Law (s 18). Even so, the drafting should be explicit.

**Push back:** Carve out:
- fraud, dishonesty, wilful misconduct and deliberate concealment by the Seller or its representatives;
- specific indemnities;
- the tax indemnity;
- title and capacity warranties;
- covenants and Completion obligations, including the price and debt mechanics.

### 4. Cap (cl 12.1): 20% (AUD 4.8m)

The cap may be negotiable for general warranties in isolation. It becomes unacceptable when combined with the Seller's other positions, because the same cap would then also apply to title, tax and the known issues.

**Push back:**
- **General warranties:** Seek more than 20%, for example 30–35%. Treat 20% as a concession we might give in exchange for the carve-outs below.
- **Fundamental (title and capacity) and tax:** 100% of the Purchase Price.
- **Specific indemnities:** Either 100% of price or uncapped, depending on the item. They must not erode the general cap.
- **Fraud:** Uncapped.

### 5. Thresholds (cl 12.2): de minimis AUD 25,000; basket AUD 250,000, recoverable only above the basket

**Problem:** A 250k basket is about 1.04% of price, at the top end of the Seller's own claimed range. It is also a *deductible* basket: we absorb the first AUD 250,000 even after the threshold is crossed. A 25k de minimis without aggregation lets a series of related small claims escape.

**Push back:**
- Make it a **tipping basket**, so that once the threshold is reached, recovery runs from the first dollar.
- Lower the basket to about 0.5% (AUD 120,000).
- Lower the de minimis to about AUD 10,000, with related claims aggregated.
- Thresholds should not apply to fundamental, tax, specific indemnity or fraud claims.

### 6. Time limits (cl 12.3 / 13): 18 months, applied "to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise"

**Problem:** The default wording quietly pulls title, tax and indemnity claims into the 18-month period.

**Push back:**
- **General warranties:** Accept 18–24 months. A period spanning at least one full audit cycle after Completion is the key point.
- **Tax:** At least the relevant statutory amendment period plus a buffer. Typically 5–7 years.
- **Title and capacity:** 7 years.
- **Specific indemnities:** Periods tied to each risk. For example, privacy matters should run until regulatory and third-party exposure has fallen away.
- **Default rule reversed:** General limitations apply to general Warranty Claims *only*.

### 7. Fundamental / title and capacity warranties under the general cap and time limits

"Administrative simplicity" is not a reason to cap title at 20% of price. If title fails, we have paid AUD 24m for less than we bargained for.

**Reject.** Title and capacity warranties should be capped at 100% of price, run for 7 years, and sit outside the de minimis, basket and disclosure.

### 8. Title evidence (DD-012)

The share register alone is not enough. The Disclosure Letter ([10]) itself says we have not verified it.

**Require:**
- an ASIC company extract reconciled to the register;
- the constitution, and any shareholders' agreement or rights of first refusal or pre-emption;
- confirmation that there are no options, convertible notes, SAFEs or ESOP grants (relevant to the DD-005 bonus arrangements);
- PPSR searches against both the Seller and the Company.

**Key point:** Check whether the Riverlark security includes a share mortgage or other security over the shares given by Harbourglass. If it does, a release must be delivered at Completion, not afterwards (see issue 10).

### 9. Bluefen change-control consent (cl 3 / 6.3)

**Facts:** About AUD 3.6m of FY26 revenue (~30%) comes from Bluefen. Its contract has a change-control consent clause (cl 11.2) with conditions (cl 11.3). The Disclosure Letter confirms that *no* final consent has been obtained and there is *no* evidence the conditions are satisfied. The cover letter's claim that this is "addressed" is wrong on the Seller's own disclosure.

**Problems with the Seller's mechanism:**
- "Reasonable endeavours" is too weak.
- Treating the condition as "satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent" ignores the cl 11.3 conditions. It would also accept a consent that is qualified or comes with conditions, such as repricing or new termination rights.

**Push back:**
- Make it a **condition precedent for the Buyer's benefit, waivable only by the Buyer**. The condition should require unconditional written consent from Bluefen, or consent on terms acceptable to the Buyer acting reasonably, and evidence that the cl 11.3 conditions are satisfied.
- The Seller should use all reasonable endeavours. The Buyer should approve the consent request before it goes, and have the right to attend discussions with Bluefen.
- Include a long-stop date and a Buyer termination right.
- Add a warranty that Bluefen has not given notice of termination, non-renewal or material reduction in volumes.
- Given the concentration, consider a price adjustment or earn-out / deferred component linked to Bluefen retention if consent comes with adverse terms.

### 10. Riverlark facility (cl 2 / 7): about AUD 3.2m, release "following Completion"

**Problem:** This conflicts with the debt-free/cash-free basis. The facility has a change-control clause (cl 8.1), so Completion may itself trigger a default or acceleration. If the release only arrives after Completion, the Company would be in default under a secured facility we now own, and the security would still be registered.

**Push back:**
- Treat the Riverlark amount as Debt, including accrued interest, break costs and fees, deducted from the price. It should be paid directly to Riverlark from the Completion funds flow.
- **Completion deliverables:**
  - a payoff letter, specifying the payout figure and per diem;
  - a deed of release and discharge of all security, including any share security;
  - an undertaking to lodge PPSR financing change statements, or lodgement at Completion;
  - return of title documents;
  - the cl 9.2 discharge.
- Alternatively, obtain a Riverlark waiver of cl 8.1 before Completion. Repayment at Completion remains the cleaner outcome.

### 11. DD-005 Completion bonuses: AUD 420,000, omitted from the funds flow

**Problem:** The Seller calls these "a matter for the Seller". However, the Company is the employer, so it bears the payment obligation and the on-costs. Those on-costs are not quantified and include:
- PAYG withholding;
- superannuation guarantee, if the bonuses are ordinary time earnings (likely, as bonuses tied to employment generally are);
- NSW payroll tax;
- possibly workers compensation.

If a continued-employment condition means a bonus is payable *after* Completion, the cost falls on the Company under our ownership.

**Push back:**
- Treat the bonuses plus all employer on-costs as **Transaction Costs / Debt-like items** deducted from the price. This applies whether they are payable at or after Completion.
- Payments at Completion should go through Company payroll. Amounts payable later should be held in escrow or retained.
- Obtain a specific indemnity covering any related tax or superannuation shortfall.
- Ask for the bonus agreements themselves. Confirm there are no other change-of-control or retention payments, and no equity-style rights.

### 12. Ironquay IP (cl 11.1): indemnity "limited to the specific SOW3 payment"

**Problem:** Under DD-004 cl 7.3, Project Materials transfer only on cleared payment of *every* SOW3 fee. DD-010 shows AUD 180,000 open, and there is no payment receipt or confirmatory assignment. Until all fees are paid, Ironquay may own SOW3 materials that could be embedded in the core product.

Indemnifying only the payment amount ignores the real exposures:
- infringement claims;
- injunctions;
- re-development costs;
- customer claims if the product is disrupted.

The 180k may also not be the only outstanding SOW3 fee, since the condition covers "every" fee.

**Push back:**
- **Condition precedent or Completion deliverable:**
  - evidence of cleared payment of all SOW3 fees, at the Seller's cost or deducted from the price;
  - written confirmation from Ironquay that nothing further is owed;
  - an executed confirmatory IP assignment, with moral rights consents where relevant.
- A specific indemnity for **all Loss** relating to Ironquay and SOW3 IP ownership. It should sit outside the cap, basket, time limits, disclosure and knowledge exclusion, or have its own high cap and a long period.
- Clarify through technical diligence which SOW3 materials are in production code.

### 13. DD-006 export / privacy incident (cl 4.6 / Schedule 6)

**Facts:** A download link was sent to an unintended external email address. The export may contain about 1,240 records: names, business emails, roles and activity timestamps. It is unknown whether anyone accessed the file, and the scope and any notification obligation have not been determined. The Seller calls this "not expected to be material". The Disclosure Letter says the investigation is only preliminary.

**Concerns:**
- **Notifiable Data Breaches scheme:** Under the *Privacy Act 1988* (Cth), an entity that suspects an eligible data breach must complete a reasonable and expeditious assessment, generally within 30 days. The disclosure is dated 22 September and it is now 5 November. We need to know when the incident was discovered and whether the assessment window has passed. Paperbark's status as an APP entity and the date it became aware are threshold questions.
- **Customer contracts:** The data may belong to customers, possibly including Bluefen. Customer contracts may impose their own notification duties and liabilities.
- **Penalties:** The penalty and enforcement framework has been strengthened recently. Regulatory exposure should not be assumed to be minor.

**Push back:**
- **Information request:**
  - the full incident timeline;
  - forensic and access logs;
  - the recipient's identity, any response, and any deletion confirmation;
  - the NDB assessment and notification decision;
  - customer communications;
  - whether insurers have been notified.
- A specific indemnity for all Loss from the incident, including regulatory penalties to the extent legally indemnifiable, investigation, notification and remediation costs, and third-party and customer claims. It should sit outside the general limitations and the knowledge exclusion.
- A pre-Completion covenant requiring the Seller to complete the assessment and make any required notifications, in consultation with the Buyer.
- Add privacy and cyber warranties, with this incident specifically disclosed but not general carve-outs.

### 14. Sandbar supplier renewals: three × AUD 110,000 (AUD 330,000 aggregate)

**Problem:** The Disclosure Letter says to read DD-008 and DD-011 "together for timing/scope". That points to one commitment possibly split into three, each below a threshold. The threshold could be one in the conduct-of-business covenant, a material contracts definition, or internal approval limits. "Related" also needs clarifying: related to each other, or a related-party arrangement? The Seller does not say whether the renewals are terminable, unavoidable, accrued or prepaid. Calling them "ordinary course" is an assertion, not a fact.

**Push back:**
- Ask for the documents, renewal dates, termination rights and any relationship between Sandbar and the Seller or its affiliates.
- If the renewals were entered or renewed after the accounts date or locked period, or outside the ordinary course, require one of:
  - Buyer consent;
  - termination before Completion at the Seller's cost; or
  - treatment of unaccrued committed amounts as Debt-like.
- Tighten the conduct-of-business covenant so related commitments are aggregated when applying thresholds.
- If any related-party element exists, treat it as leakage or Debt and add a related-party warranty.

### 15. Office lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009)

The Seller's description that these involve "notification only" and "no consent on share sale" should be checked against the underlying documents, not accepted as stated.

**Action:**
- Many leases and commercial contracts treat a change in control as an assignment. Review both definitions of assignment.
- Make any lease notification a pre-Completion covenant or Completion deliverable.
- If either document does contain a change-of-control trigger, add it to the consents conditions.

### 16. Tax and IP "under the general regime"

**Reject.**
- **Tax:** Require a standalone tax indemnity or covenant for pre-Completion tax, including tax arising from the bonuses and any payroll tax or superannuation shortfall. It should be capped at 100% of price, with a 5–7 year period, conduct-of-claims provisions, and no general disclosure.
- **IP:** For a SaaS target, the IP warranties should be fundamental or near-fundamental, with an elevated cap and a longer period. This is especially important given Ironquay. They should cover ownership of the code, open-source compliance, and employee and contractor assignments.

### 17. Credit support

Harbourglass is a ventures vehicle that may distribute sale proceeds soon after Completion.

**Seek:**
- an **escrow or retention**, for example 10% of price for 18–24 months, plus specific holdbacks for Ironquay and DD-006; and/or
- a parent guarantee.

Note that W&I insurance, if we pursue it, will typically exclude known and disclosed matters. That means everything above must still be covered by the Seller directly.

## Indicative exposure from known items

| Item | Amount | Proposed treatment |
|---|---|---|
| Riverlark debt | ~AUD 3.2m plus interest and break costs | Debt; paid out at Completion |
| DD-005 bonuses | AUD 420k plus on-costs | Debt-like / Transaction Costs |
| Ironquay SOW3 | AUD 180k (minimum) plus IP risk | Paid pre-Completion plus specific indemnity |
| Sandbar renewals | Up to AUD 330k | Investigate; Debt-like or terminate if not ordinary course |
| DD-006 incident | Unquantified | Specific indemnity plus escrow |
| Bluefen | ~AUD 3.6m revenue p.a. at risk | Condition precedent; possible price or earn-out protection |

About **AUD 4.1m of identifiable amounts** sit outside the Seller's proposed funds flow or warranty regime, before the Bluefen and privacy risks are counted. That is roughly 17% of price, close to the Seller's entire proposed cap.

## Summary of recommendations

1. **Do not accept the "FINAL" framing.** Confirm internally what, if anything, principals agreed.
2. **Delete the buyer-knowledge exclusion (cl 8.3),** or limit it to the actual knowledge of named individuals. It should never apply to indemnities.
3. **Replace general disclosure with specific, Fairly Disclosed matters.** No updating disclosure at Completion that cures a breach.
4. **Carve out from all limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance:** fraud, fundamental warranties, tax, specific indemnities and covenants.
5. **Split the liability regime by claim type:**
   - General warranties: a cap above 20%, a tipping basket of about 0.5%, a de minimis of about AUD 10k with aggregation, and 18–24 months.
   - Title, capacity and tax: 100% of price, 7 years for title, 5–7 years for tax.
   - Specific indemnities: their own terms.
6. **Bluefen:** A Buyer-waivable condition precedent requiring unconditional consent and satisfaction of the cl 11.3 conditions, with all reasonable endeavours, a long-stop date and a termination right.
7. **Riverlark:** Repay from the price at Completion, with a payoff letter, deed of release and PPSR discharge as Completion deliverables. No post-Completion release.
8. **Bonuses:** Deduct the AUD 420k plus all on-costs as Debt-like items, with a tax indemnity.
9. **Ironquay:** Payment of all SOW3 fees and a confirmatory IP assignment before Completion, plus a full-Loss specific indemnity.
10. **DD-006:** A full information request, a pre-Completion covenant to complete the NDB assessment, a specific indemnity, and an escrow holdback.
11. **Sandbar:** Investigate whether the renewals were split and whether there is a related-party element. Treat them as Debt-like or require termination if not ordinary course, and aggregate commitments in the conduct-of-business covenant.
12. **Title:** Independent verification through ASIC, PPSR (including any share security) and the constitution.
13. **Lease and Mossvale:** Verify the change-of-control definitions ourselves, and make the lease notification a Completion deliverable.
14. **Credit support:** A general escrow or retention plus specific holdbacks, and/or a parent guarantee.
15. **Refresh diligence:** Obtain all data room additions since 22 September 2026.

*These views are based only on the Seller documents provided. The underlying DD documents and the full SPA draft should be reviewed to confirm them. NSW-qualified counsel should sign off the final positions, particularly on enforceability, the Privacy Act notification timing, and payroll tax and superannuation treatment.*
